title: Si: anodized mesoporous-silicon storage node multiplies capacitor area
idea: Electrochemically anodize a 1-2 um silicon layer under the array into 5-10 nm mesopores, then ALD-coat TiN/ZrO2/TiN so each storage node is a sponge instead of one etched pillar; a 30x30 nm footprint captures ~10-30 pores and ~20-50x its planar area.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reaches 5+ fF without a 60-75:1 plasma etch, removing the hardest etch/deposition steps; per-cell pore-count variation is the main risk.

title: Al: self-ordered anodic alumina pores replace EUV for capacitor holes
idea: Deposit a thick Al film over the cell array and two-step anodize it so the oxide self-organizes into a hexagonal nanopore lattice (pitch ~25-40 nm set by anodizing voltage, AR >100), registered by shallow pre-indents from the bit-line grid; the pores become the capacitor holes and the Al2O3 is the mold.
why: Hits the AR~115 needed for more charge (fact 1) with a wet electrochemical bath instead of an EUV layer plus a deep dry etch (fact 4); aluminum is abundant and U.S.-sourced.

title: Ti: SnO2-seeded rutile TiO2 reaches k≈100 without ruthenium
idea: Use a 1-2 nm rutile SnO2 seed (isostructural, made of abundant tin) so ALD TiO2 crystallizes as rutile (k~90-170) at <=400 C instead of anatase (k~40), with ~1% Al doping to pin leakage; this replaces scarce Ru/RuO2 templates.
why: Delivers the k~70 escape route of fact 1, letting pillar AR fall from ~70:1 toward ~35:1 at the same 5 fF; cuts etch time and a scarce metal.

title: Fe: hematite Néel-vector bit flipped by titanium orbital torque
idea: Store the bit in the Néel vector of a ~5 nm alpha-Fe2O3 island, switch it with orbital-Hall current from an adjacent Ti strip (light-metal orbital torque instead of Pt/W spin-Hall), and read it by spin-Hall magnetoresistance or a stacked tunnel junction; antiferromagnetic order has no stray field and switches in picoseconds.
why: Non-volatile, field-immune, unlimited-endurance cell removes refresh (fact 3) and neighbor disturb (fact 9) using only Fe, Ti and O; a read signal of ~0.1-1% is the hurdle.

title: Zn: MgZnO/ZnO quantum-well charge bucket under a sense channel
idea: Deposit a ZnO quantum well clad by Mg0.3Zn0.7O barriers (conduction-band offset ~0.4-0.6 eV) beneath a thin oxide read channel; electrons parked in the well screen the channel and shift its threshold, so retention comes from a band offset rather than a thick capacitor dielectric.
why: Replaces the capacitor (facts 1, 2) with a low-temperature, BEOL-stackable heterostructure of abundant Zn and Mg for many 3D tiers; defect-assisted leakage out of the well is the risk.

title: Sn: SnS in-plane ferroelectric sheet stores bit as rectification direction
idea: Use few-layer SnS (abundant Sn and S), whose ferroelectric polarization lies in the sheet plane, between two lateral electrodes; the polarization direction makes one Schottky contact lower than the other so the junction rectifies left or right, read non-destructively with a small bias.
why: Non-volatile, capacitor-free bit in a 2D sheet that can be laminated into many 3D tiers (fact 2) without vertical capacitors; switching speed and SnS air stability are open.

title: C: pre-buckled amorphous-carbon nanobeam snaps between two stable shapes
idea: Deposit a 5 nm x 80 nm a-C:H (diamond-like carbon) bridge under built-in compressive stress so it buckles up or down; an electrostatic pulse from an under- or over-electrode snaps it across (GHz-class resonance gives ~1 ns transit) and the gap capacitance or tunneling current reads it.
why: Elastic bistability holds the bit with zero leakage: no refresh (fact 3), no charge wall (fact 1), carbon from methane PECVD; stiction and fatigue over 1e15 cycles are the risks.

title: N: boron-alloyed AlN ferroelectric replaces the 70:1 capacitor pillar
idea: Use sputtered Al(1-x)B(x)N (no scandium), whose remanent polarization ~100-130 uC/cm2 is ~15-20x the charge density a linear DRAM dielectric holds at 1 V; a planar 40x40 nm capacitor switches ~3-4 fC, close to a 70:1 pillar's 5 fC, sensed as in 1T1C FeRAM.
why: Removes the high-AR pillar (fact 1) and its etch tools (fact 4); B, Al and N are abundant with U.S. boron; the high coercive field (~4-6 MV/cm) and fatigue must be engineered down.

title: O: topotactic oxygen shuttle toggles CaFeO2.5 insulator and CaFeO3 metal
idea: Place a ~5 nm brownmillerite CaFeO2.5 layer against an oxygen-reservoir oxide; a field pulse fills or empties its pre-ordered vacancy channels so the whole film converts topotactically to metallic perovskite CaFeO3 and back, read as a 10-100x resistance change.
why: Uniform phase conversion through ordered channels avoids the random filaments of ReRAM, removing forming and most variability; all Ca/Fe/O; ns switching and endurance are unproven.

title: Na: Prussian-white nanocell stores bit as sodium electrochemical potential
idea: Each cell is a ~20 nm solid-state sodium couple of two Prussian-blue-analogue electrodes (Na, Fe, C, N) across a thin Na+ conductor; a write moves a few hundred Na+ ions, and the bit is the resulting ~0.3 V open-circuit voltage sensed on a read-transistor gate.
why: The bit is a thermodynamic potential, not a leaking charge, so electronic leakage does not erase it and refresh disappears (fact 3); all elements abundant; ion transit at ns and self-discharge are the risks.

title: Mg: MgB2 flux-quantum loops for 20 K helium-free memory
idea: Pattern nanoscale MgB2 loops (Tc 39 K, made only of Mg and B) that each trap zero or one flux quantum of persistent current, written by a pulsed bias line and read by a kinetic-inductance sensor, cooled to 20 K by cryocoolers (no liquid helium) beside cryogenic AI accelerators.
why: Zero-leakage, attojoule-class bits with no refresh (fact 3) and tiny data-movement energy (fact 5); avoids niobium and helium chokepoints; loop inductance limits density and cooling adds overhead.

title: Ca: mayenite electride cages trap electrons as lattice-site anions
idea: Use a thin crystalline C12A7 (Ca12Al14O33) film, whose sub-nanometre cages host electrons as anions, as the storage layer of a gate stack; a gate pulse loads or empties cages near the interface and the caged electrons shift the read transistor's threshold.
why: Electrons sit in designed, identical lattice cages rather than random defects, aiming at trap-like retention without the oxide wear that limits flash endurance; all abundant Ca/Al/O; cage stability under cycling is speculative.

title: S: CaS:Eu,Sm electron-trapping film read by on-chip light
idea: Coat each cell with ~50 nm of CaS:Eu,Sm electron-trapping phosphor; a blue micro-LED or electrical injection pushes electrons into Sm traps (write), and an infrared pulse releases them as Eu emission detected by an under-cell photodiode (destructive read, as in DRAM).
why: Deep (~1 eV) traps give long retention with no capacitor (fact 1) and no access-leakage path (fact 3); Ca and S are abundant and the rare earths are trace dopants; on-chip optical I/O speed is the hurdle.

title: H: bistable hydrogen site at Si/SiO2 interface as atomic bit
idea: Engineer a dense array of identical hydrogen defects that have two metastable configurations (bond-centred vs antibonding site, DX-like bistability); a field pulse moves the proton between sites, changing the local charge and a nearby nanowire's conductance.
why: The bit is one atom's position, giving density far beyond 6F² with no charge to leak (facts 1, 3, 4); reproducibility and room-temperature barrier height are speculative.

title: K: drifting potassium ions in gate oxide as threshold memory
idea: Deliberately dope a 4-6 nm SiO2 gate layer with K+ (the classic mobile-ion contaminant) and drive the ion cloud to the top or bottom interface with +/-3 V pulses; ion position shifts the read FET threshold ~0.3-0.5 V, and heavy ions cannot tunnel away like electrons.
why: Turns a historic reliability defect into refresh-free storage (fact 3) with an abundant element and standard oxide tools; ion drift time at ns pulses and sealing against thermal drift are the risks.

title: Mn: Mn4N ferrimagnetic racetrack shifts domain-wall bits at km/s
idea: Build racetracks from Mn4N (only Mn and N, perpendicular anisotropy, near-compensated so walls move ~1-3 km/s) and shift domain-wall-encoded bits past one read/write port with current pulses, so tens of bits share a single access transistor.
why: Amortizes access transistors and periphery (fact 7) over many bits with no capacitor (fact 1) for a large density gain; free of rare earths and cobalt; shift reliability is the risk.

title: Ni: Ni(OH)2 pseudocapacitive storage node stores tens of times more charge
idea: Coat the storage electrode with 2-3 nm of Ni(OH)2 and a thin solid proton conductor so a write drives faradaic Ni2+/Ni3+ redox, whose pseudocapacitance (hundreds of uF/cm2) is tens of times a high-k dielectric (~7 uF/cm2); the charge dumps onto the bit line like a normal DRAM read.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): a planar or low-AR node holds 5+ fF; nickel is widely available; redox rate at ~10 ns and electrolyte leakage are the risks.

title: B: sliding-ferroelectric bilayer hBN stores bits in stacking order
idea: Use parallel-stacked bilayer hexagonal BN, whose interlayer polarization flips when one layer slides by a third of a bond length (AB to BA), as a gate dielectric; the stacking state shifts the channel threshold and is read non-destructively.
why: Sliding switching moves no ions, so fatigue should be very low; no capacitor; B and N are abundant with U.S. borate supply; aligned wafer-scale bilayer growth is the risk.

title: Zr: hafnium-free ZrO2 antiferroelectric with built-in bias as bit
idea: Sandwich pure antiferroelectric ZrO2 between electrodes of different work function (e.g., TiN and a Ti-Al alloy) so the double hysteresis loop shifts and one loop straddles zero, giving two stable zero-bias states with a large field-induced switching charge as the signal.
why: AFE endurance (>1e11-1e12) beats ferroelectric HZO and avoids scarce Hf, giving a non-volatile bit with no tall pillar (facts 1, 3); holding the imprint stable over temperature is the risk.

title: Ba: BaTiO3 negative-capacitance layer boosts series storage capacitance
idea: Stack a thin BaTiO3 ferroelectric in series with the cell's linear ZrO2 and tune thicknesses so the ferroelectric runs on its stabilized negative-capacitance branch; the series stack then exceeds the linear capacitor alone, giving more charge per area at the same voltage.
why: Raises Cs at fixed AR (fact 1) or keeps charge at lower voltage (fact 10); Ba and Ti are abundant; whether quasi-static negative capacitance is stable and hysteresis-free is contested.

title: Cr: Cr2O3 magnetoelectric antiferromagnet written by voltage, not current
idea: Use a thin boron-doped Cr2O3 layer whose antiferromagnetic domain is selected by a voltage pulse under a small fixed bias field (magnetoelectric E-times-H switching), read via its boundary magnetization by anomalous Hall in an adjacent film or a stacked tunnel junction.
why: Write energy is displacement current only (~fJ), non-volatile with no refresh (facts 3, 10); chromium is abundant; boron doping must lift the Néel temperature above chip temperature.

title: Si: Coulomb-blockaded 3 nm silicon dot holds exact electron counts
idea: Shrink the storage node to a ~3 nm silicon dot whose single-electron charging energy (>100 meV, far above kT) blocks tunneling unless the gate is pulsed; the bit is 0 or N electrons, so leakage becomes a rare discrete event instead of a continuous drain, read by an integrated single-electron transistor.
why: Turns the access-leakage tail (fact 3) into Coulomb-gap-suppressed escape and lets the node scale to atomic size (fact 4); room-temperature dot-size variability is the risk.

title: N: silicon-nitride waveguide loop recirculates bits as light
idea: Hold 64 WDM channels x 100 Gb/s in a ~1.5 m spiral of ultralow-loss Si3N4 waveguide (~10 ns round trip, ~64 kbit per loop), regenerated by an on-chip amplifier every pass, so any bit is reachable from a loop tap within ~5 ns on average.
why: Sits beside co-packaged optical I/O of AI accelerators and avoids electrical data movement (fact 5) with only Si and N and no capacitor; density per mm² is low, so it fits as a bandwidth tier.

title: Si: 20:1 pillars at 1.5 fF accept 1% sense misses
idea: Cut the silicon-supported capacitor to 20:1 (~1.5 fF) and run the sense amp at ~2.3 sigma margin, which misreads ~1% of cells, then protect each 512-bit burst with an on-die LDPC code of ~12% overhead that brings output BER below 1e-15.
why: Removes about two thirds of the capacitor etch/deposit height and lets the pitch shrink (facts 1, 4); net cost per bit falls an estimated 20-30% even after ECC overhead.

title: Si: buried-channel CCD charge loops replace per-bit access transistors
idea: Store bits as charge packets circulating in 64-256-stage buried-channel silicon CCD loops clocked by three-phase gates (the 1970s CCD-memory idea revived at 12 nm), with one injector and one sense node per loop; charge-transfer loss and dark current are allowed to reach ~1% packet errors per circuit, corrected by a per-loop code.
why: No access transistor, contact or capacitor per bit (facts 1, 3, 7): a stage is just overlapping gates; the 1% budget allows faster clocking and longer loops, so average access stays ~30-60 ns.

title: Al: AlN acoustic delay loop recirculates bits as phonons
idea: Launch bits as 10 GHz acoustic pulses into a folded AlN/Al2O3 acoustic waveguide where sound travels ~10 km/s, so a 1 mm loop holds ~1,000 bits for 100 ns; a piezo transducer reads and rewrites each bit per pass, and soft-decision regeneration absorbs ~1% raw symbol errors from dispersion and noise.
why: A capacitor-free, transistor-light storage element of Al, N and O; sound is ~30,000x slower than light, so bits pack ~30,000x tighter than an optical loop, which suits streaming KV-cache traffic (fact 5).

title: Ti: adhesion-latched TiN nanorelay holds bit by van der Waals
idea: A 10 nm TiN cantilever is pulled into contact with the storage pad and held by surface adhesion with no power, then released by a reverse-polarity pull-off pulse; the ~1% of cells that stay stuck or fail to latch per scrub interval are treated as erasures by the code.
why: Zero-leakage, refresh-free bit (fact 3) from CMOS-standard TiN, where stiction, the classic NEMS killer, is used as the latch and its failures are budgeted instead of engineered out.

title: Fe: iron-triazole spin-crossover nanoparticles store bits as spin state
idea: Fill each cell with a few 10 nm [Fe(Htrz)2(trz)] spin-crossover particles whose low-spin and high-spin states coexist inside a thermal hysteresis loop near chip temperature; a current pulse flips the spin state, changing conductance ~10x, and particle spread causing ~1% misreads is absorbed by majority voting across three cells.
why: Molecule-scale non-volatile storage from Fe, C, N and H synthesized in a flask, with no high-AR etch (facts 1, 4); switching speed and cyclability are the open questions.

title: Zn: indium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cell stores three bits per node
idea: Use a ZnSnO (no In, no Ga) two-transistor gain cell whose ultralow off-current holds 8 charge levels on the read-transistor gate; level spacing is squeezed until ~1% of symbols land one level off, which a Gray-coded soft-decision LDPC per row corrects.
why: Three bits per cell triple density with no capacitor (facts 1, 2) and avoid scarce indium and gallium; the 1% tolerance is what makes 8 levels possible on a noisy oxide channel.

title: Sn: back-end complementary oxide latch from p-SnO and n-ZnO
idea: Stack a cross-coupled four-transistor latch of p-type SnO and n-type ZnO thin-film transistors in the back-end wiring, tens of tiers high; the latch needs no refresh, and SnO's poor hole mobility and variability are allowed to create ~1% weak cells that a row code corrects.
why: Static, refresh-free storage (fact 3) stacked in 3D at <=400 C over logic using abundant metals; accepting weak p-channel devices is what makes oxide CMOS usable as memory.

title: C: ten-fullerene cluster charge bit sensed through a silicon nanowire
idea: Self-assemble ~10 C60 molecules per cell on a thin tunnel oxide over a silicon nanowire; each fullerene accepts one electron at a sharp LUMO level and the bit is the collective threshold shift; with only ~10 electrons per bit, shot noise and molecular dropouts give ~1% errors that the code absorbs.
why: The storage node shrinks to ~5 nm with molecule-defined, identical charge levels, far below a 6F² capacitor (facts 1, 4); carbon comes from soot-derived fullerenes.

title: N: volatile SONOS with 1.5 nm tunnel oxide, direct-tunnel writes
idea: Thin the SONOS bottom oxide to ~1.5 nm so electrons enter the Si3N4 trap layer by direct tunneling in ~10 ns at ~2 V (no Fowler-Nordheim damage, so endurance can approach 1e12+), accept ~seconds retention with ~1% early-decay cells, and refresh at that interval.
why: Capacitorless 1T storage (facts 1, 2) from the most standard fab materials, stackable in 3D NAND-like strings; the 1% budget sets the refresh interval by the bulk, not the worst-case tail.

title: O: single oxide-trap occupancy in a tiny FinFET as bit
idea: Use the random-telegraph trap that ultra-scaled transistors carry: one oxide trap near the channel whose occupancy shifts Vt by ~20-50 mV; set it with a gate bias, read via drain current, map out devices without a usable trap at test, and accept ~1% thermal flips per refresh window.
why: Atomic-scale storage inside a minimal transistor with no capacitor (facts 1, 4), turning device noise into a bit; only viable because 1% stochastic capture errors are allowed.

title: Na: big-capacitor LTPS DRAM on soda-lime glass in idle LCD fabs
idea: Build 1T1C DRAM with low-temperature poly-Si transistors and large planar capacitors on soda-lime glass (SiN barrier against Na+) in depreciated Gen-6/8 LCD lines at 1-2 um rules; a 2.8 m2 Gen-6 panel holds ~1e11 cells (~10 GB after periphery), and panel defect densities that would kill logic are fine because <=1% bad cells are mapped and coded out.
why: Uses already-paid-for display capital instead of $15B fabs (capital intensity) with no high-AR etch (fact 1) and no EUV (fact 4); a bulk-capacity tier for AI servers.

title: Ca: polycrystalline Ca3Ti2O7 hybrid-improper ferroelectric, grain spread tolerated
idea: Sputter Ca3Ti2O7, whose polarization arises from coupled octahedral rotations (low coercive field, no Pb, Hf or Zr), as a polycrystalline capacitor film; random grain orientation widens the Pr spread, and cells with too few aligned grains (~1%) are corrected by the code instead of demanding epitaxy.
why: Non-volatile 1T1C with no pillar (fact 1), all abundant elements and a low-temperature, non-epitaxial process (fact 4); film behaviour below 20 nm is unproven.

title: Cu: CaCu3Ti4O12 colossal-k barrier-layer dielectric for flat capacitors
idea: Use CCTO, whose internal grain-boundary barrier layers give an apparent k of 1e3-1e4, as the cell dielectric so a planar or 5:1 capacitor reaches 5 fF; its lossy, grain-dependent leakage would doom a standard cell, but a 1% weak-cell budget plus faster refresh of flagged rows absorbs it.
why: Attacks the capacitor wall (fact 1) with ~100x k, eliminating the deep pillar etch; Ca, Cu, Ti and O are all abundant; barrier-layer response must survive ns timescales (major risk).

title: Mn: rare-earth-free τ-MnAl nanomagnets run deliberately volatile like DRAM
idea: Build perpendicular MTJ free layers from tau-phase MnAl (Mn and Al only, no Co, Pt or rare earths) sized for thermal stability ~25 instead of ~60, giving seconds-to-minutes retention with ~1% thermal flips between scrubs; write current drops ~2-3x and the cell shrinks.
why: Volatile MRAM as a DRAM replacement with unlimited endurance, non-destructive read (fact 8) and no capacitor (fact 1); tolerating 1% flips is what lets stability, write energy and size fall.

title: Ni: permalloy vortex-core polarity flipped by gigahertz pulses
idea: Store the bit as the up/down polarity of the vortex core in a 50-100 nm Ni80Fe20 disk, switched in ~100 ps by a short resonant in-plane current pulse and read by a tunnel junction over the core; ~1% of disks that nucleate a wrong state or chirality are absorbed by the code.
why: Topologically protected, non-volatile spin bit from abundant Ni and Fe without Co or Pt, fast enough for DRAM-class access (facts 3, 10); disk size limits density.

title: Fe: bacteria-grown greigite magnetosomes self-assemble into magnetic bit arrays
idea: Harvest near-monodisperse 40-80 nm Fe3S4 (greigite) magnetosomes from magnetotactic bacteria and dock them by magnetic self-assembly into a pre-patterned spin-orbit-torque crossbar, one particle per site; the ~1% of sites left empty or doubly filled are mapped out as erasures.
why: Bio-fabricated storage elements grown at room temperature with no lithography for the bit itself (fact 4), from abundant Fe and S; docking accuracy and read speed are major unknowns.

title: H: proton-intercalated MoO3 cell holds 16 analog levels for AI
idea: Gate a MoO3 channel through a thin phosphosilicate-glass proton electrolyte so each 5 ns pulse inserts a fixed dose of H+, giving 16 conductance levels; AI weights and KV-cache values are stored natively analog, and ~1% level errors are absorbed by the network's own noise tolerance.
why: Four bits per cell with no capacitor and in-place analog reads (facts 1, 5, 8); molybdenum is mined in the U.S.; retention drift and update symmetry are the risks.

title: F: fluorinated ferroelectric-nematic liquid crystal fills each storage well
idea: Fill nanoscale wells with a fluorinated ferroelectric nematic liquid crystal (DIO-type, polarization ~5 uC/cm2, coercive field ~1,000x below oxide ferroelectrics) so the bit is the polar director orientation switched at ~1 V; fluid order cannot fatigue like a crystal, and anchoring defects that randomize ~1% of wells are tolerated.
why: Non-volatile, low-voltage polar storage (fact 10) filled by inkjet instead of ALD; switching speed of liquid crystal confined in nanowells is the main physics risk.

title: Si: 100-tier deposited polysilicon floating-body cells, grain leakage tolerated
idea: Deposit alternating poly-Si/oxide layers as in 3D NAND and form capacitorless floating-body cells whose stored holes set the threshold; grain-boundary leakage makes ~1% of cells retain too briefly, which the code covers, so no single-crystal Si/SiGe epitaxy or wafer bonding is needed.
why: Opens 3D DRAM beyond the ~26-tier break-even (fact 2) on existing 3D NAND toolsets; the 1% tolerance is what makes cheap polysilicon acceptable.

title: H: hydrogen-lithographed silicon dangling-bond pairs hold single-electron bits
idea: On an H-terminated Si(100) surface, remove single hydrogen atoms to leave paired dangling bonds that share one extra electron on either side; the electron's side is the bit, set by local gates, and ~1% thermally hopped pairs per refresh window are corrected.
why: Atomic-pitch (~1 nm) storage attacks density and lithography cost at the floor (fact 4); capping and room-temperature operation make it speculative.

title: S: tetrathiafulvalene rotaxane monolayer crossbar with defect-mapped molecular switches
idea: Sandwich a monolayer of bistable [2]rotaxanes between nanoimprinted crossbar wires at ~15 nm pitch; oxidizing the sulfur-rich tetrathiafulvalene station shuttles the ring and changes junction conductance, and a defect map plus code tolerates ~1% dead or shorted junctions.
why: Crossbar of molecules gives ~4F² density with no per-bit transistor or EUV (fact 4); switching speed (us-ms) and endurance are the gap to DRAM-class, so it starts as a dense slow tier.

title: N: silicon-nitride nanostring parametron stores bit as oscillation phase
idea: Pump GHz Si3N4/AlN nanomechanical resonators (Q~300) at twice resonance so each settles in ~100 ns into one of two oscillation phases, 0 or pi, as in Goto's 1950s parametron; one frequency comb pumps thousands of resonators, and phase slips up to ~1% per hold interval are corrected by the code.
why: Dynamical bistability needs no stored charge, so there is no leakage tail (fact 3) and no capacitor (fact 1); pump power is the cost.

title: Si: JEDEC AI-grade memory class admitting 1% raw cell errors
idea: Define a JEDEC grade for AI weights and KV cache in which devices may ship with up to 1% raw cell BER, the controller carries a standardized LDPC/erasure layer, and buyers get a guaranteed post-correction error rate; DRAM dies now scrapped or down-binned for weak cells, and every leaky or low-margin new cell, become sellable.
why: Raises usable supply immediately through several points of yield and gives constrained cell technologies a legal market, cutting capital and scarce-resource use per usable bit.
